current_question: Let's set aside the guessing scenario for a moment. Suppose instead you already have the 5 students' actual exam scores in front of you—say, 70, 75, 80, 85, and 90. Now, if you had to pick just one single number to serve as your best guess for *all five* of these known scores at once, what number would you choose, and what would make it the "best" choice compared to other numbers you could pick?

user_input: Well that would be the mean, or the empty model. This number reduces the residual error of all the students' score (it balances residual error to 0). While that doesn't always make the mean the best choice, it is an unbiased measure.

current_question: Now let's push into another area. Suppose I have a group model instead—say, I'm predicting exam scores based on whether a student studied or not, so I calculate the mean score separately for the "studied" group and the "didn't study" group. Thinking about SS Total, SS Model, and SS Error: if I only had the empty model (the overall mean) versus this new group model, how would the SS Total compare between the two models, and why?

user_input: The SS total should stay exactly the same. This is because SS total is just equal to SS given by the empty model. To see how much better the studied model is, you want to look at SS model, which is the amount of error reduced by the model.

user_input: You are subtracting the mean for that group depending on your explanatory variable. In the case of studied versus didn't study, you are subtracting the group mean from each student's score depending on which category they fall into. It doesn't matter which explanatory variable you are using, you are always subtracting the number generated by the model to find residual error.
